The creosote endures. The Marble Mountains to our north endure. The San Bernardino Mountains are still hours ahead, still invisible, rising out there beyond the afternoon haze. The basin floor continues to unspool, pale and immense.

The ground out both windows right now is recent work — geologically speaking, yesterday. Quaternary sediments, laid down inside the last two and a half million years, washed off the mountain flanks and sorted themselves out here on the basin floor. Sand and gravel and silt, still only loosely cemented. The Mojave doesn't hide its skeleton. No topsoil worth mentioning, no canopy to screen it. What you're seeing is the raw arithmetic of a desert: runoff arrives, drops its load, and evaporates. The alluvium keeps coming. It's building the floor even now.
units.place: Open Mojave floor, San Bernardino County

units.text: We're in the dead center of San Bernardino County, the largest county in the lower forty-eight by area — bigger than nine states. Two million people live here, but nearly all of them are stacked into the western end, around the cities. Out here the county is mostly silence and shrub and the occasional set of parallel lines — the railroad, the highway, the ghost of the highway before it. Every corridor technology of the last two centuries threaded this same trough: the pack-mule trails, then the telegraph, then steel rail, then asphalt. The Mojave didn't give them options. The basin floor is the only navigable seam through the ranges, and so each generation of movers simply overlaid itself on the last. We're riding that palimpsest right now.

Before you can see the ruins, the name tells the story. Ash Hill is named for a Southern Pacific surveyor — Benjamin Ash — who died here in the desert while staking the route. A man died; they named a water stop for him; the water stop grew into a railroad siding; the siding attracted a community; the community died when through-traffic moved on. That's the biography of nearly every settlement we pass along this corridor. The railroad giveth, and the railroad — or the highway that superseded it — taketh away. Ash Hill is the sixth or seventh such place we've passed today, each one following the same arc with minor variations.

This stretch of desert in the 1880s was one of the most strategically contested railroad corridors in the American West. The Southern Pacific had built first, and for a decade it had a stranglehold on California freight rates. The Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe was fighting to break that monopoly, driving its own line west through this same basin. The two roads raced and wrangled, building sidings and water tanks every dozen miles — not because the desert demanded them, but because passengers and steam locomotives demanded water at roughly the same intervals. Every one of those tank stops became a named place. Every named place is now, or is becoming, a ghost. Ludlow is the next one.

Ludlow started in 1883 — the same year the railroads imposed standard time zones on the country — as a watering stop on the Atlantic and Pacific line, a Santa Fe subsidiary pushing west. Watering stop became depot, depot attracted a general store, the store attracted a borax-trade connection from the Calico Mountains to the north, and for a few decades Ludlow was something. Then Route 66 arrived and gave it a second life as a gas stop, a diner. Then Interstate 40 bypassed it and the diner closed and the gas pumps went dark and the old ghost-town logic reasserted itself. The ruins of the Route 66 Ludlow sit a few hundred yards off the interstate. The historic structures are still there — just no longer in use. Water, motion, commerce: when the flow reroutes, the town drains.

Here's the math on water in the Mojave. Annual precipitation in this part of the basin: four to five inches. Los Angeles, a hundred and fifty miles west, gets fifteen. Kansas City, where some of us started two days ago, gets forty. Each hundred miles we traveled west of the Continental Divide the rainfall thinned in a rough gradient, and we felt it — the grass shortened, the trees disappeared, the soil went pale. Four inches isn't enough to support agriculture without irrigation. It's barely enough to support the creosote flats we've been watching. Creosote spaces itself geometrically across the desert floor, each plant's root system claiming exactly as much territory as it needs. What looks like random scatter is a map of water rights.

Around milepost 2050 the bedrock shifts — the geology turns Pliocene, older than the Quaternary sediments we've been riding over. Coarser alluvium, some lake deposits, remnants of water bodies that existed here when the climate was wetter. Ancient playas, the ghosts of Pleistocene lakes. The fossils pulled from this county make the past strange and vivid: Dyseohyus fricki, a pig-like creature from sixteen million years ago. Gopherus agassizii — the desert tortoise, essentially unchanged, still out there in the scrub. White pelicans. Grebes. Birds of open water, fossilized in a place that now gets four inches of rain a year. The water was here. It left. Everything that followed is adaptation to that departure.

Off to the left — you'll want to look — that low dark cone rising above the lava plain is Pisgah Crater. A cinder cone, young in volcanic terms, with the last eruption perhaps ten thousand years ago, which means humans were already here when it blew. The lava field spreading around it, black and fractured and jagged, is so fresh-looking the Army used it for astronaut training before the Moon landings. The rock hasn't had time to weather into soil. Nothing colonizes it yet except the toughest desert plants working the cracks. Pisgah is a reminder that the Mojave isn't simply an old, eroded landscape waiting quietly. The earth here is restless on a timescale longer than history but shorter than geology's usual patience.

The Fred Harvey Company understood something about this landscape that the railroad surveyors didn't: people needed a story to travel into it. The desert wasn't selling itself. Harvey's solution, from the 1880s onward, was to put a Harvey House — a clean dining room, a curated menu, Harvey Girls in starched white aprons — at strategic railroad stops through exactly this kind of terrain. You could step off the train in the middle of the Mojave and sit down to a properly laid table. Harvey didn't just sell meals; he sold the idea that the West was manageable, approachable, worth the discomfort of getting there. The Southwest Chief still follows the Harvey stops, though the Harvey Houses are mostly gone or converted. The architecture of reassurance has its own ghosts now.

Hector is barely a place — a railroad siding name on the map, no services, no structures worth noting from the train. But the name is in the atlas, which means at some point it mattered enough to somebody to put it there. The Mojave scatter-plots these named nothings across the map. Each one is a small monument to the ambition that the railroad corridor briefly inflated and the desert ultimately deflated.

We're past the segment's high point now — a summit near milepost 2065 at about 2,165 feet — and on a long, gradual descent toward the Mojave Valley and Barstow. The Mojave River is out there to our north, running underground for most of its length. One of the desert's subsurface rivers: water that soaks into the sand immediately after a rain and travels invisibly toward the basin. The Mojave River is why Barstow exists. It's why prehistoric peoples settled in this basin. Surface water is so rare here that an underground flow becomes the organizing principle of entire civilizations' geography.

The geology under us shifts again near milepost 2090 — Pliocene volcanic, intermediate composition, the remnants of a more active period before the basin-and-range stretching pulled the crust apart and quieted most of the eruptions. Intermediate volcanic means something between basalt and rhyolite, the product of magma that had mixed and differentiated partway. The gray-green rocky outcrops where the terrain allows. The Mojave has layers: ancient Miocene sediments at the base, Pliocene volcanics above, Quaternary alluvium on top, each layer recording a different chapter of what this basin was doing when it was laid down.

Gale — another name, another near-nothing on the modern map. The populated-places database keeps these alive even when the places themselves have contracted to a survey marker and a memory. We'll pass it without comment.

We're coming into Barstow's orbit now. The Mojave Valley opens ahead — the flat that the basin-and-range faulting carved out over millions of years. Daggett comes first, just ahead of Barstow proper. Daggett is older than Barstow; it was a silver-mining supply town in the 1880s, before the railroad consolidated traffic at Barstow. The corridor logic shifted slightly, and Barstow won, and Daggett shrank. Barstow itself sits at the confluence of the Mojave River and two rail lines — which is to say it sits at the confluence of water and transportation, which in the desert is the only kind of site that survives.

The bedrock under Daggett shifts to Miocene sedimentary rocks — older than anything we've crossed since leaving the Colorado River basin. Twenty-three million years of compressed history in the stone beneath the town. Above it: Quaternary alluvium, Route 66 asphalt, an old Harvey House that became a hotel that became a ruin. The Mojave Valley floor is wide here, pale tan, the mountains ringing it in every direction. This is the basin at its most legible — the fault-bounded trough, the alluvial fans spilling off every range, the dry wash threading the center. It's the Mojave's basic grammar, written large. Barstow, two miles ahead, is where the corridor has always caught its breath before the next climb west.

The cluster of low buildings ahead is Daggett — blink and you'll miss it, but don't. In the 1880s this was a supply depot for the silver mines working the Calico Hills to the north, a place where ore came down by twenty-mule team and left on the newly laid rails of the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad. The railroad didn't just serve the mines; it made them economically thinkable. Strip the steel away and the ore stays in the ground. Daggett today is a handful of addresses in the desert, but the logic that built it — rail as the lever that unlocks everything else — runs all the way back to Chicago.

The sediment under the wheels right now was laid down in the Miocene — the same formation that's been carrying us through the eastern Mojave. In that era the basin held shallow lakes and river floodplains; the Mojave was wetter, the basin-and-range faulting still actively corrugating the landscape. What the fossils found near here tell us: a dolphin-relative called Allodelphis, a small horse ancestor, a pig-like browser. All twenty-three million years old. All found in sediment that formed in a world this ground no longer resembles. We are crossing the inheritance of a wetter past.
Nebo — a name on a map, barely a place. Someone planted a biblical mountain in the Mojave and moved on. We keep moving too.

The Mojave River runs alongside us somewhere, but mostly underground here. It's a river that sinks into its own alluvial bed within miles of its source, percolating through gravel rather than flowing at the surface. Every settlement between Barstow and Victorville exists not because the river is visible but because it's calculable — someone worked out where the water table was shallow enough to reach by digging. Every water tank the AT&SF placed along this right-of-way was a bet on that calculation. The settlements don't follow the river. They follow the rumor of it. That arithmetic — scarce water, possible survival — is what we've been reading in the landscape for two thousand miles. Here it becomes acute.

We're pulling into Barstow — a genuine station stop, a few minutes. The town exists because the Santa Fe platted it in 1886 and named it for William Barstow Strong, the railroad's president. Before the AT&SF arrived there was only the Mojave Road, a nineteenth-century freight track used by Army mule wagons and emigrants crossing toward San Bernardino. The railroad made Barstow a division point: locomotives watered, crews changed, cars sorted. The Harvey House dining room fed the passengers while they waited. The yard is still working freight today — watch for the long strings of intermodal containers as we clear the station. The corridor keeps its grip.

The Harvey Houses deserve a real story here. Fred Harvey opened his first restaurant along the AT&SF in 1876 — Topeka, Kansas — and by the time the railroad reached California the chain had grown into something unprecedented: a system for civilizing the passenger West. White tablecloths. China plates. Fresh-baked bread. And the Harvey Girls — young women recruited from back East by newspaper advertisements that promised wages, room, board, and respectability in exchange for a year's service on the frontier. Thousands came. The AT&SF ran special recruitment cars to bring them out. The girls signed contracts promising not to marry for a year; the joke, which contained a lot of truth, was that the railroad built more frontier marriages than any matchmaker in history. More than five thousand Harvey Girls eventually married and stayed in the West. The AT&SF's marketing department knew exactly what it was doing: the Harvey system was selling the Southwest as a destination, not just a crossing. And Barstow was one of those stations where the manufactured romance and the actual gritty railroad town existed side by side, within fifty feet of each other.

Hodge sits on the Mojave River and on old Route 66, though neither distinction has kept it alive. The highway and the railroad ran parallel here for decades, car traffic and train traffic using the same river grade, the same desert corridor. When Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, places like Hodge lost their through-traffic in a single administrative act. The trains kept coming; the cars found the interstate. Hodge belongs to two eras now and fully to neither.

Before we reach Bryman, consider what this corridor is. In the 1820s Spanish traders used the Old Spanish Trail to drive horses and mules east from California, returning with woolen goods from the New Mexico missions — a route that followed the Mojave River's course to reach water in the desert. The Mormon Road of the late 1840s traced the same ground, driving cattle north from San Bernardino to the Salt Lake settlements. When American military surveyors crossed here in 1848 looking for a Pacific wagon route, they noted the same thing everyone before them had noted: the Mojave River's drainage offered the only reliable water in a sixty-mile belt of desert. When the AT&SF needed a grade to the coast in 1883, its engineers followed that water-dictated line. When highway planners laid Route 66 in 1926, they followed the railroad. The corridor is not a human invention. It is a hydrological fact — the place where a river makes the desert crossable — that human beings have been rediscovering, in succession, for two hundred years.

Bryman lies at twenty-five hundred feet, right where the Mojave River bends south toward Victor Valley. Five miles north of Oro Grande on the old Route 66 alignment. The place carried different names for different eras of travelers: a Mormon Road crossing, a stage stop, a Route 66 way station. Now almost nothing. But notice the wash to our left — the Mojave River is showing itself above ground again here, after its long underground run from Barstow. The gravel is damp. The water is surfacing as the valley narrows ahead and the water table rises to meet it.

The Victor Valley ahead is a topographic catchment, and the Mojave River concentrates here. By high-desert standards the water table is relatively shallow — shallow enough that by the early twentieth century farmers were attempting alfalfa and fruit orchards, and that by mid-century the valley was filling with suburbs for people priced out of coastal California. The same water logic that placed Serrano people here for centuries placed ranchers here in the 1890s and placed a hundred and thirty thousand exurbanites here today. The math hasn't changed. Only the population using it has grown.

To our right, behind the long perimeter fence, is the federal prison complex — USP Victorville, opened 2004 on land that was a military air base before that. Federal land, flat ground, far from coastal populations. The desert keeps drawing institutions that need space and distance. The emptiness that deterred homesteaders keeps attracting the government.

Watch the ground outside as we approach Victorville. Near milepost 2150 the bedrock transitions — from Miocene sedimentary, twenty-three million years old, to Holocene wash deposits that are geologically today, laid down by the Mojave River in essentially the present era. The same river we've been following since Barstow is also actively depositing the ground we're riding over. River, route, rock. They're the same story at different timescales, and the color of the valley floor shifts subtly as the older pale-buff sediments give way to the lighter, looser recent gravels near the active channel.

Victorville — 134,000 people by the 2020 census, named for Jacob Nash Victor, a construction superintendent on the California Southern Railroad who pushed the line through here in 1885. Incorporated 1895 — the same decade the great cattle drives were winding down and barbed wire was finishing the enclosure of the open range. The railroad town grew into a junction point, then a Route 66 stop, then a postwar affordable-housing exurb for people who couldn't reach the coast. Today it's home to a federal prison, a regional airport on the old George Air Force Base grounds, and a hundred and thirty thousand people who commute over Cajon Pass when they can. The corridor made this city. The corridor still defines it.

We're crossing a boundary now that's been building for two thousand miles. The bedrock shifts from Miocene sedimentary to Early Pleistocene alluvial-fan deposits — two and a half million years old, remnants of ancient fans that spilled off the San Bernardino mountain front when the range was rising fast. Look ahead. The mountains are fully visible now. The San Bernardinos are fault-bounded, lifted by the San Andreas system, and the front face we're approaching is one of the steepest mountain walls in the lower forty-eight: eleven thousand feet of relief in less than fifteen miles of horizontal distance. We've been in those mountains' rain shadow for this entire desert crossing. The Mojave gets eight inches of rain a year. The peaks above Cajon Pass get forty. Once we clear the pass, the Pacific weather comes back. The long dry lesson is almost over. The last Holocene wash deposits under us are the final chapter of the Mojave Basin — the living river still writing the ground.

Hesperia — Greek for the western land, the country of the setting sun. Poets used it for Italy, then Spain, then wherever the known world ended. Now it's a California city of nearly a hundred thousand people on Early Pleistocene alluvial fans at the foot of the mountain wall, incorporated 1988, still growing. The Holocene wash gravels of the valley floor give way here to those older, consolidated fan deposits — slightly reddish in the afternoon light, pressed hard by two million years of weight. The mountain front is close ahead. In ten miles we enter Cajon Pass, and the desert ends. The Pacific is on the other side.

Out to the right, Oak Hills spreads across the high desert flats of the Victor Valley — low rooftops, creosote still pushing through between the cul-de-sacs. This is Mojave Basin and Range at its most unresolved: not city, not wilderness, just the unfinished edge where the desert simply runs out of room. The alluvium we're crossing right now is ancient fan debris, cemented sand and gravel pushed off the mountains two and a half million years ago, now holding up subdivisions. The water that deposited it is long gone. The people who moved here brought theirs in pipes.

The corridor we've been riding since Chicago was never just a railroad. Long before the AT&SF laid track through here in the 1880s, this same general alignment was already a path — the Mojave Road, a desert crossing used by Southern Paiute traders and Spanish missionaries, then by U.S. Army survey parties. When Lieutenant Edward Beale pushed a wagon road through in 1857, using camels — actual camels, imported from Egypt on a War Department experiment — he was following the same logic every traveler before him had: this is where the mountains open, this is where water can be found, this is the way through. The railroad engineers didn't invent the route. They just buried it in steel.

Watch the cut banks and road exposures out either side — the rock is changing. We've rolled off the Pleistocene alluvial fans and into something far older. What you're seeing now, where the land rises toward Cajon Pass, is Cretaceous intrusive rock: granite and related igneous stone that cooled deep underground when dinosaurs were still alive. One hundred and forty-five to sixty-six million years old. Not deposited, not layered — crystallized, slowly, miles beneath whatever surface existed then. The uplift that eventually cracked California exposed it. We're driving over the roots of a vanished mountain range.

Cajon Pass — just ahead and to our left — is the reason this railroad exists here at all. The San Gabriel and San Bernardino mountains rise on either side of us, granite walls topping seven and eight thousand feet, and Cajon is one of the few low slots through the Transverse Ranges: the only practical grade a locomotive can negotiate without tunneling for miles. The Santa Fe won a bitter race with the Southern Pacific to get here first, arriving in 1885. Before that, the Mormon Trail came through Cajon in the 1850s — wagons and mule teams grinding down the canyon wall on ropes. Before that, the Spanish called it the pass to the valley. The water running through it — Cajon Creek, draining the San Bernardinos — isn't much to look at, but it was everything: the reason every traveler since the Serrano people has aimed at this gap.

Lytle Creek comes off the San Gabriel Mountains to the right. Small stream, big history. In 1851 — the Gold Rush still roaring — a detachment of soldiers under Amos Lytle was sent up this canyon to find a lost immigrant party. They found the canyon instead and the name stuck. What the canyon holds, more importantly, is water: real, reliable, mountain-fed water percolating down through the alluvial fan into aquifers beneath the Inland Empire. The communities downstream — San Bernardino, Riverside, the whole basin — sit on a geological accident: a natural underground reservoir trapped between mountain blocks, recharged by snowmelt off peaks that top eight and nine thousand feet. That aquifer is why this valley was farmable. Why the citrus grew. Why anyone stayed.

The land opening to our right was, a hundred years ago, wall-to-wall citrus — navel oranges, mostly, in long ruled rows all the way to the mountains. The Santa Fe didn't just build through here; it sold the orange. Starting in the 1880s, the railroad ran refrigerator cars east under the brand "California on Wheels," delivering oranges to Chicago and New York that had been picked in the groves we're passing through. The California Fruit Growers Exchange — which became Sunkist in 1919 — was a marketing machine as much as a farming co-op. They invented the word "Sunkist." They ran ads telling Americans that drinking orange juice was modern, healthy, Californian. The railroad made it possible. The marketing made it necessary. The demand filled this valley with groves within a generation.

Muscoy to the right — a small, unincorporated neighborhood tucked against the north edge of San Bernardino. Ten thousand people, census-designated place, census-ignored community. A lot of the Inland Empire is like this: places with enough people to fill a small city, not enough political weight to become one. The orange groves are condominiums now.

San Bernardino's story runs so deep it has multiple founding dates depending on whose story you tell. The Mormons established a colony here in 1851, buying rancho land from Mexican grantees who'd themselves taken it from the Serrano and Cahuilla people living in the valley. The Mormon settlement lasted barely four years before Brigham Young recalled the colonists to Utah — 1857, when he feared federal military pressure and needed every hand. The town they left behind was real enough that it kept going, incorporated as a city in 1854 in the middle of the colony, refounded by incoming Californians after the Mormons left. By the time the Santa Fe arrived in 1883, San Bernardino was already a working city. The railroad didn't create it. It just made it the junction for everything that came after.

San Bernardino station, left side. The AT&SF depot has been here since 1918 — Mission Revival style, tile roof, arched arcade — built in the idiom the Santa Fe used to sell the Southwest as romantic, civilized, desirable. Fred Harvey ran the restaurant here. The building that stands now is smaller than the original, but the bones are right. Pause if you can, look back at it as we pull away. This was the nerve center of Santa Fe operations in Southern California for a century. The yard behind it still moves freight. We're at 1,077 feet — we've dropped more than two thousand feet since we crested the terrain east of Victorville this morning. The basin opens ahead of us now, flat, hot, enormous.

The Inland Empire — the name dates to the 1890s, when Riverside boosters coined it to distinguish their prospering basin from the coastal cities — sits in what geologists call a structural depression, a down-dropped block between the San Bernardino Mountains to the north and a series of lower ranges to the south. It's a basin catching sediment and catching water. The Santa Ana River drains it westward; before dams and groundwater pumping, it flooded regularly. The orange empire that made this region famous was built on flood-irrigated fields and artesian wells — wells that sometimes flowed without pumping because the aquifer was under pressure from the mountain snowmelt above. By 1900 Riverside had the highest per-capita income of any city in the United States. Not manufacturing, not industry. Oranges. Water. A mountain range acting as a cistern. The aridity that made the desert a barrier had been turned, here, into an engine.

Riverside station, left side. The city was platted in 1870 by a Canadian colony company that wanted to sell California citrus land to settlers who'd never seen it. They brought the Washington Navel orange — a Brazilian variety, propagated from two parent trees planted in 1873 by Eliza Tibbets, who got her cuttings from the U.S. Department of Agriculture — and within a decade this valley was producing oranges that were changing American eating habits coast to coast. One of those original Tibbets trees still stands in a traffic median in downtown Riverside. Every navel orange you've ever eaten traces its ancestry to that Brazilian cutting, planted in this valley, on aquifer water, in Cretaceous granite soil. The railroad carried the story east. The story sold the land.

We're crossing into Riverside County now — a county of two and a half million people, nearly all of them in what used to be farmland, groves, and desert. The land cover here is essentially all developed: one of those census facts that lands differently when you're looking out the window at the sprawl spreading to the horizon in every direction. The mountains that built this basin, that gave it water, that made it fertile — they're still visible to the north, blue and clear, the San Bernardinos holding their snowpack through spring. The relationship between those peaks and this pavement is the whole story of Southern California in one view.

Casa Blanca appears ahead — a neighborhood of Riverside now, annexed decades ago, but once a separate community with its own identity, largely Mexican-American, working families who came to pick and pack the citrus the boosters were selling east. The labor that built the orange empire was mostly invisible in the marketing — the Fred Harvey menus didn't mention who harvested the fruit. Casa Blanca was where the workers lived. The groves are gone. The neighborhood remains.

The geology beneath us has shifted one more time. Around milepost 2220 we'll be riding over Middle Pleistocene alluvial fans again — younger than what we crossed this morning east of the mountains, laid down roughly twelve thousand to eight hundred thousand years ago, the San Bernardino Mountains shedding debris as they rose along the San Andreas fault system just to our north. That fault, the boundary between the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate, runs roughly parallel to our track for miles. The mountains we're leaving behind are being lifted by it right now, invisibly, imperceptibly — about an inch a year. In geologic terms, a sprint. In human terms, the slow engine that made the pass, made the basin, made the water, made the corridor we've been riding since Chicago.

Corona–West Metrolink station comes up ahead — a commuter rail stop on what was once only the AT&SF main. The Inland Empire feeds workers into Los Angeles and Orange County every morning on these tracks. The corridor that carried buffalo hides east and orange crates west now carries people in both directions, daily, in numbers that would have astonished the first Santa Fe surveyors standing in Cajon Pass in 1876 trying to figure out if they could get a train through at all. They could. We just did. Ahead, the basin flattens, the density thickens, and the Pacific begins to pull us west.

The train slows through Corona, and if you watch the platform you'll see Metrolink commuters — the daily pulse of the inland empire running on the same rails the Santa Fe laid through here in the 1870s. Different passengers, same corridor. These 91-line trains fan out to Riverside and back; we angle west toward the coast. The bedrock under us right now is a Middle Pleistocene alluvial fan — river-dumped gravel and sand laid down somewhere between 780,000 and 12,000 years ago, when the San Bernardino Mountains were shedding sediment into the basin at a rate the modern landscape barely hints at.

That phrase — Middle Pleistocene alluvial fan — is worth sitting with, because it's doing a lot of work under our wheels. The Pleistocene was the great ice-age epoch, running from roughly 2.6 million years ago down to about 12,000 years back. "Middle" Pleistocene means the slice between 780,000 and 120,000 years ago. While glaciers locked up water to the north, Southern California ran cooler and wetter — rivers here ran harder and longer, and every mountain storm built enormous fan-shaped aprons of debris spreading out from the canyon mouths. The gravel under Corona and Riverside is that debris: sorted by water, compacted by time, capped now by those rust-red clay layers — argillic horizons, the soil scientists call them — where iron and clay have slowly migrated downward over tens of thousands of years and locked in place. We've been riding these fans since we left the San Bernardino foothills. Around mile 2230, the fans give way to Miocene sedimentary rock underneath. A different chapter entirely.

Coming up ahead — just outside Yorba Linda — the Yorba Hacienda. You won't see much from the window, but the name carries weight. Bernardo Yorba built this place on the Rancho Cañón de Santa Ana, a Mexican land grant covering tens of thousands of acres. In the 1830s and '40s the Yorba family was the wealthiest in Alta California. They ran cattle on land that now holds four cities and roughly 800,000 people. The grant system — huge parcels given by the Mexican government to prominent families — shaped the entire Southern California landscape. When California entered the Union in 1850, American courts spent decades adjudicating these grants. The families mostly lost. The Yorbas' land fragmented. The place names survive — Yorba Linda, Cañón de Santa Ana — while the cattle range is long gone under suburb.

In 1887, the Santa Fe and the Southern Pacific were in the middle of a rate war so aggressive that a ticket from Kansas City to Los Angeles dropped to one dollar. One dollar. The resulting land boom was unlike anything California had seen: within a year, dozens of towns were platted across Orange and Los Angeles Counties, many of them funded or promoted directly by the railroad. Citrus groves were the pitch — the idea that any midwesterner with modest savings could buy five acres and retire in perpetual Southern California sunshine picking oranges. The Santa Fe's advertising posters showed a landscape nothing like the alluvial fans and scrub we're crossing. They showed paradise. Some of those orange-grove towns held. Many did not. All of them were built on a marketing department as much as on any natural abundance. What the railroad sold was California itself — a manufactured vision of ease at the end of a long, hard journey.

Fullerton — we stop here. The Southwest Chief shares this platform with the Pacific Surfliner and two Metrolink lines. The city was founded in 1887 — the same year the Santa Fe completed its line through here, the same year of that dollar fare. George Fullerton, the railroad's land agent, gave his name to the place. The company's method: buy the land ahead of the surveyors, build the railroad, plat the town, sell the lots. Repeat across the entire Southwest. We're leaving Orange County now. Ahead: Los Angeles County, the most populous county in the United States — nearly ten million people, more than forty individual states. The city is pulling us in.

Around milepost 2240 we move onto Holocene alluvium — the youngest deposits on this whole segment, laid down in the last 12,000 years. The Santa Ana River and its tributaries have been building this flat coastal plain since the last glacial period ended and sea level stabilized. Loose stuff: silt, sand, cobbles still moved by water that floods this plain in wet winters. The aridity gradient that governed everything from eastern Kansas to the Mojave resolves here, where the Pacific moderates the climate and the mountains catch enough winter rain to keep rivers running. The long dry logic of the interior West runs out at the coast. Under the freeways and warehouse districts, the ground is still a river's unfinished business.

La Mirada off to our right — one of the Gateway Cities on the Orange-Los Angeles county line. In the 1950s and '60s this was the edge of expansion: suburban tracts absorbing workers from the aerospace plants and auto assembly lines that defined the postwar Los Angeles economy. Most of those plants are gone. The housing stock from that era remains, slightly aging, home now to a working population that looks nothing like the families who moved in during the boom years. The land changes slowly. The people on it change faster.

Route 66 ran through this basin — the Mother Road, designated 1926, decommissioned 1985. For most of this leg we've been roughly parallel to it, or crossing it, or riding track the highway later mimicked. The Santa Fe preceded Route 66 by fifty years in this corridor. When the highway came, it followed the same logic: lowest passes, reliable water, existing towns. Then the Interstate Highway Act of 1956 began its own work — the freeways absorbed the Route 66 traffic, and the towns that the highway had sustained started to thin. We've watched that sequence across two thousand miles: trail becomes railroad becomes highway becomes freeway. Each generation of infrastructure enabling and obsoleting the last. Here in the Los Angeles basin, all four layers exist simultaneously. You can almost see them stacked, out the window, right now — the old AT&SF alignment, the Route 66 surface street running parallel, the freeway overpass above it.

Montebello to our right — eight miles from downtown. The name means "beautiful mountain" in Italian, though the mountains are mostly haze today. The Tongva people lived along the San Gabriel River here for thousands of years. Spanish missions reorganized the landscape in the 1770s. The missions became ranchos, the ranchos became subdivisions, and the oil fields that made early Montebello wealthy in the 1910s are mostly capped under commercial streets. Each economy invisible now beneath the next.

Commerce — population 12,000, but one of the larger industrial footprints in the county. The city incorporated in 1960 specifically to capture factory tax revenue and avoid annexation by Los Angeles. A common strategy along this corridor in the postwar boom: cities drawing their borders around warehouse districts rather than neighborhoods. The freight rail visible to our right still moves container traffic from the ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles eastward — the same corridor we rode from Chicago now carries goods moving the other direction, Pacific trade flowing inland. The Santa Fe's trade flows are still active. Just different containers at different speeds.

Two miles from Union Station. The geology under us is Quaternary sediment — the accumulated outflow of every river and stream that has ever drained the San Gabriel and Santa Monica Mountains into this basin. Hundreds of feet deep in places. Los Angeles is built on its own geological debris, on material the mountains have been shedding since before the first human crossed into the Western Hemisphere. We came west on a corridor defined first by indigenous trails, then by the Santa Fe Trail, then by a railroad, then by Route 66, then by the interstates. The corridor ends at the Pacific, in a basin made of mountains, in a city made of borrowed water. Union Station in two minutes. The train is slowing.

lore.title: Cicero, Illinois
lore.summary: Cicero is a town in Cook County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2020 census, the population was 85,268, making it the 11th-most populous municipality in Illinois. The town is named after Marcus Tullius Cicero, a Roman statesman and orator. With a population more than 89% Hispanic, the town is the most Hispanic in the state of Illinois.

lore.title: Cook County, Illinois
lore.summary: Cook County is the most populous county in the U.S. state of Illinois and the second-most-populous county in the United States, after Los Angeles County, California. More than 40 percent of all residents of Illinois live within Cook County. As of 2020, the population was 5,275,541. The county seat is Chicago, the most populous city in Illinois and the third most populous city in the United States. The county is at the center of the Chicago metropolitan area.

lore.title: Hinsdale, Illinois
lore.summary: Hinsdale is a village in DuPage County, Illinois, United States, with a small portion in Cook County. It is one of the wealthiest communities in Illinois and in the United States. Hinsdale is a western suburb of Chicago with a population of 17,395 in the 2020 census.

lore.title: Naperville, Illinois
lore.summary: Naperville is a city in DuPage and Will counties in the U.S. state of Illinois. It is a city southwest of Chicago located 28 miles (45 km) west of the city on the DuPage River. As of the 2020 census, its population was 149,540, making it the state's fourth-most populous city.

lore.title: Aurora, Illinois
lore.summary: Aurora is a city in northeastern Illinois, United States, located along the Fox River. The population was 180,542 at the 2020 census. It is the second-most populous city in Illinois, after Chicago, and the 144th-most populous city in the US. Aurora is the most populous city in Illinois that is not a county seat.

lore.title: Yorkville, Illinois
lore.summary: Yorkville is a city within the Chicago metropolitan area and the county seat of Kendall County, Illinois, United States. It is a suburb of Chicago, Illinois. The population was 23,835 as of the 2022 census.

lore.title: Plano, Illinois
lore.summary: Plano is a city in Kendall County, Illinois, United States, with a population of 11,847 as of the 2020 census. It is part of the Chicago metropolitan area, being about 55 miles (90 km) from Chicago. The city was home to the Plano Harvester Company in the late 19th century, as well as the Plano Molding Company more recently. In 2011, downtown Plano was used as a set for Man of Steel.

lore.title: Sandwich, Illinois
lore.summary: Sandwich is a city in DeKalb and Kendall counties in the U.S. state of Illinois. Its population was 7,421 at the 2010 census and 7,221 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Leland, Illinois
lore.summary: Leland is a village in LaSalle County, Illinois, United States. The population was 951 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Ottawa Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Earlville, Illinois
lore.summary: Earlville is a city in LaSalle County, Illinois, United States. The population was 1,613 at the 2020 census, down from 1,701 at the 2010 census. The city is part of the Ottawa, IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Mendota, Illinois
lore.summary: Mendota is a city in LaSalle County, Illinois, United States, in the state's north-central region. The population was 7,061 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Ottawa, IL Micropolitan Statistical Area. Mendota is located approximately 85 miles (137 km) west of Chicago, 70 miles (110 km) east of Moline and 55 miles (89 km) south of Rockford. The current mayor is David W. Boelk, an independent elected to a four-year term.

lore.title: Dover, Illinois
lore.summary: Dover is a village in Bureau County, Illinois, United States. The population was 135 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Ottawa Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Buda, Illinois
lore.summary: Buda is a village in Bureau County, Illinois, United States. The population was 482 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Ottawa Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Neponset, Illinois
lore.summary: Neponset is a village in Bureau County, Illinois, United States. The population was 427 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Ottawa Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Kewanee, Illinois
lore.summary: Kewanee is a city in Henry County, Illinois. "Kewanee" is the Winnebago word for greater prairie-chicken, which lived there. The population was 12,509 in the 2020 census, down from 12,916 in 2010.

lore.title: Galva, Illinois
lore.summary: Galva is a city in southern Henry County, Illinois, United States. The population was 2,470 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Altona, Illinois
lore.summary: Altona is a village in Knox County, Illinois, United States. The population was 463 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Galesburg Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Galesburg Township, Knox County, Illinois
lore.summary: Galesburg Township is one of twenty-one townships in Knox County, Illinois, USA. As of the 2020 census, its population was 406 and it contained 175 housing units.

lore.title: Cold Brook Township, Warren County, Illinois
lore.summary: Cold Brook Township is located in Warren County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2010 census, its population was 467 and it contained 196 housing units.

lore.title: Warren County, Illinois
lore.summary: Warren County is a county in the U.S. state of Illinois. According to the 2020 census, it had a population of 16,835. Its county seat is Monmouth.

lore.title: Media, Illinois
lore.summary: Media is a village in Henderson County, Illinois, United States. The population was 121 at the 2020 census, up from 107 at the 2010 census. It is part of the Burlington, IA–IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Henderson County, Illinois
lore.summary: Henderson County is a county located in the U.S. state of Illinois. According to the 2020 United States census, it has a population of 6,387. Its county seat is Oquawka. Henderson County is part of the Burlington, IA–IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Lomax, Illinois
lore.summary: Lomax is a village in Henderson County, Illinois, United States. The population was 404 at the 2020 census, a decline from 454 in 2010 census. It is part of the Burlington, IA–IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Fort Madison, Iowa
lore.summary: Fort Madison is a city in and a county seat of Lee County, Iowa, United States along with Keokuk. Of Iowa's 99 counties, Lee County is the only one with two county seats. The population was 10,270 at the time of the 2020 census. Located along the Mississippi River in the state's southeast corner, it lies between small bluffs along one of the widest portions of the river. Fort Madison is also the home of the Iowa State Penitentiary.

lore.title: Nauvoo Township, Hancock County, Illinois
lore.summary: Nauvoo Township is one of twenty-four townships in Hancock County, Illinois, USA. At the 2020 census, its population was 963 and it contained 667 housing units.

lore.title: Wade Branch
lore.summary: Wade Branch is a stream in Clark County in the U.S. state of Missouri. It is a tributary of the Fox River.

lore.title: Medill, Missouri
lore.summary: Medill is an unincorporated community and census-designated place in Clark County, in the U.S. state of Missouri. As of the 2020 census, its population was 82.

lore.title: Railroad Lake
lore.summary: Railroad Lake — a reservoir in Clark County, MO.

lore.title: Fabius, Missouri

lore.title: La Plata station
lore.summary: La Plata station is an Amtrak train station in La Plata, Missouri, United States, served by the daily Southwest Chief. It was built in 1945 by the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway as a replacement for an 1887-built, 1888-opened passenger and freight depot that was in deteriorating condition. Efforts to replace the station were stalled by a lack of construction material during World War II. The 1945 replacement was built in Art Deco style, and was restored between 1996 and 2001 by local preservationists, a model railroad club, and a garden club. The station was upgraded again in 2022 with upgrades done to the station building and the platform to bring it into compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act. It also hosts two Virtual Railfan cameras.

A variant name was Evelyn, the name of the local post office. A post office called Evelyn was established in 1888, and remained in operation until 1916. Besides the post office, Hart had a railroad depot.

lore.title: United States Post Office (Carrollton, Missouri)
lore.summary: U.S. Post Office is a historic post office building located at Carrollton, Carroll County, Missouri. It was designed by the Office of the Supervising Architect under James Knox Taylor and built between 1910 and 1912. It is a two-story, rectangular, Renaissance Revival style building constructed of regular coursed, smooth cut, Missouri limestone. It has a low hipped roof of red tile and features two large round arched windows flanking the main entrance.

lore.title: Farmers Bank Building (Norborne, Missouri)
lore.summary: Farmers Bank Building, also known as the Citizens Bank of Norborne, is a historic bank building in Norborne, Carroll County, Missouri. It was built c. 1892, and is a two-story, Romanesque Revival style brick and cut-stone commercial building measuring 58 feet by 75 feet.

lore.title: Hardin, Missouri
lore.summary: Hardin is a city in southeast Ray County, Missouri, and part of the Kansas City metropolitan area within the United States. The population was 571 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Lexington, Missouri
lore.summary: Lexington is a city in and the county seat of Lafayette County, Missouri, United States. As of the 2020 census, Lexington had a population of 4,652. Lexington is in western Missouri, within the Kansas City metropolitan area, approximately 40 miles (64 km) east of Kansas City. It is the home of the Battle of Lexington State Historic Site, and of the former Wentworth Military Academy and College, which operated from 1880 to 2017.

lore.title: Wellington, Missouri
lore.summary: Wellington is a city in Lafayette County, Missouri, and part of the Kansas City metropolitan area within the United States. It is located approximately 35 miles east of Kansas City. As of the 2020 census, Wellington had a population of 738.

lore.title: Buckner, Missouri
lore.summary: Buckner is a city in Jackson County, Missouri, United States. The population was 2,945 at the 2020 census. For decades it was best known for TV and radio commercials promoting local automobile dealership Lasater Ford, run by the Lasater brothers, Wilson and Milton and later Halverson Ford. It is part of the Kansas City metropolitan area.

lore.title: Missouri City, Missouri
lore.summary: Missouri City is a city in Clay County, Missouri, United States. The population was 217 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Kansas City metropolitan area.

lore.title: Independence, Missouri
lore.summary: Independence is a city mostly in, and one of two county seats of, Jackson County, Missouri, United States. It is a satellite city of Kansas City, Missouri, and is the largest suburb on the Missouri side of the Kansas City metropolitan area. In 2020, it had a total population of 123,011, making it the fifth-most populous city in Missouri. A small part of the city extends into Clay County.

lore.title: University of Kansas School of Medicine
lore.summary: The University of Kansas School of Medicine is a public medical school located on the University of Kansas Medical Center campuses in Kansas City, Kansas, and also Salina, Kansas, and Wichita, Kansas. The Kansas City campus is co-located with the independent University of Kansas Health System, and they are commonly known collectively as KU Med.

lore.title: Argentine, Kansas
lore.summary: Argentine is a community of Kansas City, in the southern part of Wyandotte County, Kansas, United States. It is bordered on the west by the Turner community, on the east by the Rosedale community, on the south by Johnson County, and on the north by Armourdale community and by the Kansas River.

lore.title: De Soto, Kansas
lore.summary: De Soto is a city along the Kansas River, in Johnson and Leavenworth counties in the U.S. state of Kansas, and part of the Kansas City Metropolitan Area. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 6,118, and the 2025 estimate is 7,083.

lore.title: Eudora, Kansas
lore.summary: Eudora is a city in Eudora Township, Douglas County, Kansas, United States, along the Kansas and Wakarusa rivers. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 6,408.

lore.title: Lawrence, Kansas
lore.summary: Lawrence is a city in and the county seat of Douglas County, Kansas, United States, and the sixth-largest city in the state. It is in the northeastern sector of the state, astride Interstate 70, between the Kansas and Wakarusa rivers. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 94,934. The city is a college town with a significant student population, because it is home to both the University of Kansas (KU) and Haskell Indian Nations University (HINU).

lore.title: Perry, Kansas

lore.title: Topeka, Kansas

lore.title: Wakarusa, Kansas

lore.title: Carbondale, Kansas
lore.summary: Carbondale is a city in Osage County, Kansas, United States. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 1,352. It is located south of Topeka along the U.S. Route 75 four-lane freeway.

lore.title: Osage County, Kansas
lore.summary: Osage County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kansas. Its county seat is Lyndon, and its most populous city is Osage City. As of the 2020 census, the county population was 15,766. The county was originally organized in 1855 as Weller County, then renamed in 1859 after the Osage tribe.

lore.title: Lyon County, Kansas
lore.summary: Lyon County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kansas. Its county seat and largest city is Emporia. As of the 2020 census, the county population was 32,179. The county was named for Nathaniel Lyon, a general who was killed at the Battle of Wilson's Creek during the Civil War.

lore.title: Emporia, Kansas
lore.summary: Emporia is a city in and the county seat of Lyon County, Kansas, United States. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 24,139. Emporia lies between Topeka and Wichita at the intersection of highways K-99, U.S. Route 50, Interstates 335 and 35. It is home to Emporia State University and Flint Hills Technical College, and two annual sporting events: Unbound Gravel and Dynamic Discs Open.

lore.title: Saffordville, Kansas
lore.summary: Saffordville is an unincorporated community in Chase County, Kansas, United States. It is located approximately halfway between Strong City and Emporia near the intersection of U.S. Route 50 highway and Zz Rd. BNSF Railway passes through the community.

lore.title: Cottonwood Falls, Kansas
lore.summary: Cottonwood Falls is the largest city in and the county seat of Chase County, Kansas, United States. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 851. It is located south of Strong City along the south side of the Cottonwood River.

lore.title: Strong City, Kansas
lore.summary: Strong City is a city in Chase County, Kansas, United States. Originally known as Cottonwood Station, in 1881 it was renamed Strong City after William Barstow Strong, then vice-president and general manager, and later president of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 386. It is located along U.S. Route 50 highway.

lore.title: Chase County, Kansas
lore.summary: Chase County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kansas. Its county seat and most populous city is Cottonwood Falls. As of the 2020 census, the county population was 2,572. The county was named for Salmon Chase, a U.S. Senator from Ohio that was a Kansas statehood advocate. It is best known for the book PrairyErth: A Deep Map, a book written during, and partially about, the discussion within the county about the establishment of the Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve. It is one of several areas in Kansas that utilize prescribed burning for the maintenance of pastureland.

lore.title: Cedar Point, Kansas
lore.summary: Cedar Point is a city in Chase County, Kansas, United States. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 22. It is approximately five miles east of Florence and 0.5 mile south of U.S. Route 50 highway.

Newton is located 25 miles (40 km) north of Wichita. The city of North Newton. located immediately north, exists as a separate political entity. Newton is located at the intersection of Interstate 135, U.S. Route 50, and U.S. Route 81 highways.

lore.title: Burrton, Kansas
lore.summary: Burrton is a city in Harvey County, Kansas, United States. It is named after Isaac T. Burr, former vice-president of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 861.

lore.title: Hutchinson, Kansas
lore.summary: Hutchinson is the largest city in and the county seat of Reno County, Kansas, United States, and located along the Arkansas River. As of the 2020 census, the population of the city was 40,006. It has been home to salt mines since 1887, thus its nickname of "Salt City". Each year, Hutchinson hosts the Kansas State Fair, and National Junior College Athletic Association (NJCAA) Men's Basketball Tournament. It is the home of the Hutchinson Community College, the Cosmosphere aerospace museum, and Strataca underground salt museum.

lore.title: Kansas
lore.summary: Kansas is a landlocked state in the Midwestern region of the United States. It borders Nebraska to the north, Colorado to the west, Oklahoma to the south, and Missouri to the east. Kansas is named after the Kansas River, in turn named after the Kansa people. Its capital is Topeka, and its most populous city is Wichita; however, the largest urban area is the bi-state Kansas City metropolitan area surrounding Kansas City, Missouri, which straddles the border of Kansas and Missouri.

lore.title: Reno County, Kansas
lore.summary: Reno County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kansas. Its county seat and largest city is Hutchinson. As of the 2020 census, the population was 61,898. The county is named for Jesse Reno, a general during the Civil War.

lore.title: Holly SS Ranch Barn
lore.summary: The Holly SS Ranch Barn, or Double S Ranch Barn, at 407 West Vinson in Holly, Colorado, was built in 1879. It is located south of the railroad tracks on the south side of Holly.

lore.title: Lamar station (Amtrak)
lore.summary: Lamar station is a train station in Lamar, Colorado served by Amtrak. It is served by Amtrak's Southwest Chief line. It was originally built in 1907 by the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway. The current station is designed in a manner similar to that of Garden City station in Kansas, and also serves as the Lamar Visitor Center. In 2019 it was added to the National Register of Historic Places.

lore.title: Bent's New Fort
lore.summary: Bent's New Fort was a historic fort and trading post along the banks of the Arkansas River in what is now Bent County, Colorado, about nine miles west of Lamar, on the Mountain Route branch of the Santa Fe Trail. William Bent operated a trading post with limited success at the site and in 1860 leased the fort to the United States government, which operated it as a military outpost until 1867. In 1862, it was named Fort Lyon. The fort was abandoned after a flood of the Arkansas River in 1867.

lore.title: Caddoa, Colorado
lore.summary: Caddoa is an extinct town located in Bent County, Colorado, United States. The community took its name from nearby Caddoa Creek.

lore.title: John Martin Reservoir
lore.summary: John Martin Reservoir is a reservoir on the Arkansas River in Bent County in southeastern Colorado. Built and managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, it is used for flood control, irrigation, and recreation. John Martin Reservoir State Park lies on its shore.

lore.title: Bent County Courthouse and Jail
lore.summary: The Bent County Courthouse and Jail, of Bent County, Colorado, at 725 Bent Ave. in Las Animas, was built in 1887. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1976; the listing included two contributing buildings.

lore.title: Bent's Old Fort National Historic Site
lore.summary: Bent's Old Fort is a historical fort located in Otero County in southeastern Colorado, United States. A company owned by Charles Bent and William Bent and Ceran St. Vrain built the fort in 1833 to trade with Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho Plains Indians and trappers for buffalo robes. For much of its 16-year operation as a trading post, the fort was the only major white American permanent settlement on the Santa Fe Trail between Missouri and the Mexican settlements. It was initially abandoned by William Bent in 1849.

lore.title: La Junta station
lore.summary: La Junta station is a train station in La Junta, Colorado served by Amtrak. Amtrak's Southwest Chief trains 3 & 4 stop here for 10–15 minutes. Westbound trains are scheduled to arrive at 8:15 AM and depart at 8:30 AM, while the eastbound trains arrive at 7:30 PM and depart at 7:41 PM. There are no facilities at the station itself beyond a toilet and beverage vending machine. La Junta was a major point along the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway, as a branch line to Pueblo and Denver started from here.

lore.title: Tyrone, Colorado
lore.summary: Tyrone is an unincorporated community located in Las Animas County, Colorado, United States. The U.S. Post Office at Model now serves Tyrone postal addresses.

lore.title: Model, Colorado
lore.summary: Model is an unincorporated community with a U.S. Post Office in Las Animas County, Colorado, United States. The Model Post Office has the ZIP Code 81059 and has been in operation since 1912. The community originally was a planned, or "model" community, hence the name.

lore.title: Hoehne, Colorado
lore.summary: Hoehne is an unincorporated town, a post office, and a census-designated place (CDP) located in and governed by Las Animas County, Colorado, United States. At the United States Census 2020, the population of the Hoehne CDP was 80.

lore.title: Starkville, Colorado
lore.summary: Starkville is a statutory town in Las Animas County, Colorado, United States. The population was 62 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Morley, Colorado
lore.summary: Morley was a town in Las Animas County, Colorado, that existed between 1878 and 1956. The town was located near the summit of Raton Pass and was originally a railroad stop, before being developed into a coal mining town by the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company (CF&I). Morley was a CF&I company town for fifty years until 1956 when the mine was closed and the town demolished.

lore.title: Raton Pass
lore.summary: Ratón Pass is a 7,834 ft (2,388 m) elevation mountain pass on the Colorado–New Mexico border in the western United States. It is located on the eastern side of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains between Trinidad, Colorado and Raton, New Mexico, approximately 180 miles (290 km) northeast of Santa Fe. Ratón is Spanish for "mouse". The pass crosses the line of volcanic mesas that extends east from the Sangre de Cristo Mountains along the state line, and furnishes the most direct land route between the valley of the Arkansas River to the north and the upper valley of the Canadian River, leading toward Santa Fe, to the south. The pass now carries Interstate 25 and railroad tracks.

lore.title: Raton station
lore.summary: Raton is an active railroad station in the city of Raton, Colfax County, New Mexico, United States. Located at 201 South First Street, the station serves Amtrak's Southwest Chief. Connections are also available to Denver, Colorado via Amtrak Thruway bus service. The station is staffed during the summer season when tourism for the Philmont Scout Ranch and the NRA Whittington Center shooting complex is at its peak. During off-seasons, it is open at all train times, maintained by a caretaker. Passengers with layovers there often visit the non-profit Old Pass Gallery, located on the station grounds in the restored 1910 Railway Express Agency building. The station also includes a former freight depot.

lore.title: NRA Whittington Center
lore.summary: The NRA Whittington Center is one of the largest and most comprehensive shooting facilities in the United States. Owned and operated by the National Rifle Association of America (NRA), the centre is located in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains of Colfax County, New Mexico. Ten percent of the 33,300-acre (13,500 ha) site has been developed to include twenty-three shooting ranges, an administration building, a cafeteria, a museum, a library, classrooms, and full-service hookups for 175 recreational vehicles. The remainder of the site provides wildlife habitat at elevations above 6,300 feet (1,900 m) with primitive camp-grounds and remote back-country cabins for hunting, bird watching, wildlife viewing, photography, hiking, mountain biking, and horseback riding.

lore.title: Schomberg
lore.summary: Schomberg — a populated place in Colfax County, None.

lore.title: French

lore.title: Cimarron Solar Facility
lore.summary: The Cimarron Solar Facility is a 30 megawatt (MWAC) photovoltaic power station in Colfax County, New Mexico, United States. It was the largest solar facility in the state when completed in December 2010, and uses Thin-film solar panels manufactured by the U.S. firm First Solar. The electricity is being sold to Tri-State Generation and Transmission under a 25-year power purchase agreement.

lore.title: R.H. Cowan Livery Stable
lore.summary: The R.H. Cowan Livery Stable, at 220 Maxwell Ave. in Springer, New Mexico, was built in 1883. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.

lore.title: Levy

lore.title: Wagon Mound, New Mexico
lore.summary: Wagon Mound is a village in Mora County, New Mexico, United States. It is named after and located at the foot of a butte called Wagon Mound, which was a landmark for covered wagon trains and traders going up and down the Santa Fe Trail and is now Wagon Mound National Historic Landmark. It was previously an isolated ranch that housed four families that served as local traders. The shape of the mound is said to resemble a Conestoga wagon. As of the 2020 census, the village population was 266. It was also called Santa Clara for many years. The village, with brightly painted houses and several stores and shops, is located on the plains of northeastern New Mexico. Interstate 25, which skirts the western side of town, gives a view of the majority of the town. Wagon Mound is not growing rapidly, but it has seen new construction along I-25, with new buildings on the northeast side of town as well. Wagon Mound was also the site of the 1850 Indian attack, the Wagon Mound Massacre.

lore.title: Valmora, New Mexico
lore.summary: Valmora is an unincorporated community located in Mora County, New Mexico, United States. The community is located along New Mexico State Road 97, 3.75 miles (6.04 km) east-northeast of Watrous. State Road 446, the shortest state road in New Mexico at .25 miles (0.40 km), links the community to State Road 97. It was founded in 1916 when a tuberculosis sanitarium was established.

lore.title: Watrous, New Mexico
lore.summary: Watrous is an unincorporated community and census-designated place (CDP) in Mora County, New Mexico, United States. Its population was 99 as of the 2020 census, down from 135 in 2010. Watrous has a post office with ZIP code 87753, which opened on April 14, 1868. The community is located along Interstate 25. It was named after merchant and landowner Samuel Watrous, who moved to New Mexico from Vermont in 1835.

lore.title: Las Vegas Municipal Airport
lore.summary: Las Vegas Municipal Airport is five miles (8 km) northeast of Las Vegas, in San Miguel County, New Mexico.

lore.title: Castañeda Hotel
lore.summary: The Castañeda Hotel is a historic railroad hotel located in Las Vegas, New Mexico. It was built in 1898 and 1899 by the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway, and was operated by the Fred Harvey Company until 1948. After being mostly vacant for many years, the hotel was restored and reopened in 2019. The Castañeda was listed on the New Mexico State Register of Cultural Properties in 1974 and the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 as a contributing property in the Railroad Avenue Historic District. It is located adjacent to the Las Vegas railroad station.

lore.title: Ribera, New Mexico
lore.summary: Ribera is an unincorporated community and census-designated place in San Miguel County, New Mexico. Located in the northern part of the state, it is at the foot of Rowe Mesa and along the Pecos River, 50 miles (80 km) southeast of Santa Fe.

lore.title: Ilfeld, New Mexico
lore.summary: Ilfeld is an unincorporated community located in San Miguel County, New Mexico, United States. The community is located along Interstate 25's frontage road, 22.5 miles (36.2 km) southwest of Las Vegas. Ilfeld has a post office with ZIP code 87538.

lore.title: Rowe, New Mexico

lore.title: Glorieta, New Mexico
lore.summary: Glorieta is a census-designated place (CDP) in Santa Fe County, New Mexico, United States. It is part of the Albuquerque–Santa Fe–Las Vegas combined statistical area. As of the 2020 census, Glorieta had a population of 511. The community is located in the southern Sangre de Cristo Mountains, along Interstate 25 on the east side of Glorieta Pass.

lore.title: Santa Fe County, New Mexico
lore.summary: Santa Fe County is a county located in the U.S. state of New Mexico. As of the 2020 census, its population was 154,823, making it New Mexico's third-most populous county, after Bernalillo County and Doña Ana County. Its county seat is Santa Fe, the state capital.

lore.title: Galisteo, New Mexico
lore.summary: Galisteo is a census-designated place (CDP) in Santa Fe County, New Mexico, United States. It is part of the Santa Fe, New Mexico Metropolitan Statistical Area. The population was 253 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Rio Rancho, New Mexico
lore.summary: Rio Rancho is the largest and most populous city in Sandoval County, New Mexico, United States. A small portion of the city extends into northern Bernalillo County. Part of the expansive Albuquerque metropolitan area, it is the third-largest city in New Mexico, and one of the most rapidly growing. Rio Rancho had a population of 104,046 at the 2020 census. The name Rio Rancho derives from Los Ranchos, the Spanish colonial ranches established along the Rio Grande in the Albuquerque Basin, and throughout historic Nuevo México. There were large ranches also in neighboring Corrales. Since the late 20th century, it has developed as a suburb of Albuquerque.

lore.title: North Valley, New Mexico
lore.summary: North Valley is a census-designated place (CDP) in Bernalillo County, New Mexico, United States. As of the 2020 census, North Valley had a population of 11,149. It is part of the Albuquerque Metropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Bernalillo County, New Mexico
lore.summary: Bernalillo County is the most populous county in the U.S. state of New Mexico. As of the 2020 census, the population was 676,444. The county seat, Albuquerque, is the most populous city in New Mexico. Bernalillo County is the central county of the Albuquerque, NM Metropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: South Valley, New Mexico
lore.summary: South Valley is a census-designated place (CDP) and unincorporated community in Bernalillo County, New Mexico, United States. The population was 38,338 at the 2020 Census. It is part of the Albuquerque Metropolitan Statistical Area. The U.S. Postal Service uses "Albuquerque" for all South Valley addresses.

lore.title: Bosque Farms, New Mexico
lore.summary: Bosque Farms is a village in Valencia County, New Mexico, United States. The population was 4,020 in the 2020 census. It is part of the Albuquerque Metropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Los Lunas, New Mexico
lore.summary: Los Lunas is a village in Valencia County, New Mexico, United States. As of the 2020 census, the village has a population of 17,242. It is the county seat of Valencia County. Los Lunas is part of the Albuquerque metropolitan area.

lore.title: Valencia County, New Mexico
lore.summary: Valencia County is a county in the U.S. state of New Mexico. As of the 2020 census, the population was 76,205. The county seat is Los Lunas.

lore.title: Los Lunas Decalogue Stone
lore.summary: The Los Lunas Decalogue Stone is a hoax associated with a large boulder on the side of Hidden Mountain, near Los Lunas, New Mexico, about 35 miles (56 km) south of Albuquerque, that bears a nine-line inscription carved into a flat panel. The stone is also known as the Los Lunas Mystery Stone or Commandment Rock. The stone has gained notoriety in that some claim the inscription is Pre-Columbian, and therefore proof of early Semitic contact with the Americas. Standard archeological evidence contradicts this, however.

lore.title: Rio San Jose
lore.summary: The Rio San Jose is a 90-mile-long (145 km) tributary of the Rio Puerco in the U.S. state of New Mexico.

lore.title: Highland Meadows, New Mexico

lore.title: Anzac
lore.summary: Anzac — a populated place in Cibola County, None.

lore.title: Thoreau, New Mexico
lore.summary: Thoreau is an unincorporated community and census-designated place (CDP) in McKinley County, New Mexico, United States. The population was 2,367 at the 2020 census, up from 1,865 in 2010. It is majority Native American, primarily of the Navajo Nation, as Thoreau is located within its boundaries.

lore.title: Continental Divide, New Mexico
lore.summary: Continental Divide is an unincorporated community and census-designated place (CDP) in McKinley County, New Mexico, United States. It has a post office with ZIP code 87312. As of the 2020 census, it had a population of 187.

lore.title: Fort Wingate
lore.summary: Fort Wingate was a military installation near Gallup, New Mexico, United States. There were two other locations in New Mexico called Fort Wingate: Seboyeta (1849–1862) and San Rafael (1862–1868). The most recent Fort Wingate (1868–1993) was established at the former site of Fort Lyon, on Navajo territory, initially to control and "protect" the large Navajo tribe to its north. The fort at San Rafael was the staging point for the Navajo deportation known as the Long Walk of the Navajo. From 1870 onward the garrison near Gallup was concerned with Apaches to the south, and through 1890 hundreds of Navajo Scouts were enlisted at the fort.

lore.title: Gallup, New Mexico
lore.summary: Gallup is a city in McKinley County, New Mexico, United States, with a population of 21,899 as of the 2020 census. A substantial percentage of its population is Native American, with residents from the Navajo, Hopi, and Zuni tribes. Gallup is the county seat of McKinley County and the most populous city between Flagstaff and Albuquerque along historic U.S. Route 66.

lore.title: Purty Rock, New Mexico
lore.summary: Purty Rock is an unincorporated community and census-designated place (CDP) in McKinley County, New Mexico, United States. As of the 2020 census, it had a population of 163.

lore.title: Manuelito, New Mexico

As of the 2010 census, the Lupton CDP had a population of 25.

lore.title: Houck, Arizona

lore.title: Chambers

lore.title: Navajo, Arizona
lore.summary: Navajo is a populated place situated in Apache County, Arizona, United States. It has an estimated elevation of 5,676 feet (1,730 m) above sea level.

lore.title: Painted Desert Inn
lore.summary: Painted Desert Inn is a historic complex in Petrified Forest National Park, in Apache County, eastern Arizona. It is located off Interstate 40 and near the original alignment of historic U.S. Route 66, overlooking the Painted Desert.

lore.title: Adamana, Arizona
lore.summary: Adamana is an unincorporated community in Apache County in the northeast section of the U.S. state of Arizona. The town was settled in 1896 in what was then the Arizona Territory.

lore.title: Little Lithodendron Wash

lore.title: Joseph City, Arizona
lore.summary: Joseph City is a census-designated place located in Navajo County, Arizona, United States. It is located on Interstate 40, approximately eighty miles east of Flagstaff and about thirty-five miles west of Petrified Forest National Park. In 2010, there were 1,386 inhabitants.

lore.title: Manila, Arizona
lore.summary: Manila is a populated place situated in Navajo County, Arizona, United States. Its name was bestowed during the Spanish–American War, being named after the Philippines' capital.

lore.title: Homolovi State Park
lore.summary: Homolovi State Park is a state park of Arizona, United States, preserving over 300 Ancestral Puebloan archaeological sites. Homolovi or Homol'ovi is a Hopi word meaning "place of the little hills". The park is located just over a mile north of Winslow, Arizona, and features historical exhibits, interpretive programs, birdwatching, and hiking. There is a year-round campground, restrooms with showers and an RV dump station. The park was closed to visitors from February 22, 2010 to March 18, 2011 due to state budget cuts.

lore.title: Winslow, Arizona
lore.summary: Winslow is a city in Navajo County, Arizona, United States. According to the 2020 census, the population of the city is 9,005. It is approximately 57 miles (92 km) southeast of Flagstaff, 240 miles (390 km) west of Albuquerque, New Mexico, and 329 miles (529 km) southeast of Las Vegas.

lore.title: Meteor City, Arizona
lore.summary: Meteor City was a historic trading post located on historic Route 66, west of the Unincorporated town of Winslow, within Coconino County, Arizona. Accessing it from Interstate 40 (I-40), you would exit at Mile-marker / Exit 239 coming from the east or west.

lore.title: Canyon Diablo (meteorite)
lore.summary: The Canyon Diablo meteorite refers to the many fragments of the approximately 50 m (160 ft) diameter asteroid that created Meteor Crater, Arizona, United States. Meteorites have been found around the crater rim, and were named in 1891 by convention for the closest post office, Canyon Diablo, Arizona. The actual canyon lies about 2.5 miles west of the crater in the westernmost part of the strewn field.

lore.title: Two Guns, Arizona
lore.summary: Two Guns is a defunct roadside attraction near Interstate 40 in northern Arizona, United States. It is located on the east rim of Canyon Diablo in Coconino County, west of Winslow and northeast of Phoenix. This area was originally known as Canyon Lodge, but became known as Fort Two Guns with the arrival of Harry E. "Indian" Miller in the 1920s. The "Fort" was dropped in the 1930s.

lore.title: Twin Arrows, Arizona
lore.summary: Twin Arrows is a ghost town located in the central part of Arizona on U.S. Route 66 (US 66) in Coconino County between the city of Flagstaff and the town of Winslow.

lore.title: Winona, Arizona
lore.summary: Winona is a small populated place in Coconino County in the northern part of the U.S. state of Arizona. At one time it was also called Walnut, and Winona's railroad station was renamed Darling in honor of an engineer.

lore.title: Cosnino
lore.summary: Cosnino — a populated place in Coconino County, None.

lore.title: Tunnel Spring

lore.title: Bellemont, Arizona
lore.summary: Bellemont is an unincorporated community in Coconino County, Arizona, United States, located along Interstate 40, about 11 miles (18 km) west-northwest of Flagstaff. At an elevation of 7,132 feet (2,174 m), it is claimed to be the highest settlement along historic Route 66. It was a known water stop due to its local springs. As of June 2012, it had an estimated population of 893.

lore.title: Keyhole Sink
lore.summary: Keyhole Sink is a canyon in the shape of a keyhole near Williams, Arizona. The canyon is best known for its petroglyphs, which were created about 1,000 years ago by the ancient Cohonina people, and the seasonal waterfalls that flow into the canyon.

lore.title: Williams, Arizona
lore.summary: Williams is a city in Coconino County, Arizona, United States, located west of Flagstaff. As of the 2020 census, Williams had a population of 3,202. It lies on the routes of Historic Route 66 and Interstate 40. It is also the southern terminus of the Grand Canyon Railway, which takes visitors to Grand Canyon Village.

lore.title: Red Lake, Arizona
lore.summary: Red Lake is an unincorporated community and census-designated place (CDP) in Coconino County, Arizona, United States. It is bordered to the south by the city of Williams. It was first listed as a CDP prior to the 2020 census.

lore.title: Corva, Arizona
lore.summary: Corva was a populated place situated in Coconino County, Arizona. It has an estimated elevation of 6,227 feet (1,898 m) above sea level.
